## Original problem (task)
[d31d61f36df18c74] (h005.task.v1)
I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

## Selected input account (p.response.0)
[6a444f126cdfd335] (h005.fork5.p.response.0)
Source account: daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/account; selected view: both
Artifact: b03a0e344c5dafea45291832589eb85bc7b8589ca8c65e53e1f487b0b49d8e19

Delivery: COMPLETE; envelope: AUTHORED
BODY
The material exposes five facts and no interpretations: three people share a flat; they argue about chores; they sometimes agree who will do something and later disagree about what that agreement meant; their work schedules change; one friend has begun avoiding the conversations. Everything else — who does more, whether the agreements were spoken or written, why the friend avoids — is not stated, so what follows is a set of conjectures for the asker to check against what they actually know.

The most useful conjecture is that this is not primarily a fairness fight but an ambiguity problem wearing a fairness fight's clothes. An agreement that fixes who but leaves when, to what standard, and under what conditions is only half an agreement; the missing halves get filled in later by each party, sincerely and differently. That would explain the otherwise odd feature of the disputes — that they are about meaning rather than about refusal. Nobody has to be lying for this to recur; the shared record simply never existed.

The second conjecture concerns the schedules. An agreement made under one roster can become unmeetable under another, and where there is no cheap, explicit way to renegotiate, the natural move is silence — which the others will read as defiance. Some of what looks like bad faith may be changed feasibility with no exit route. This also makes the avoidance partly intelligible: if the conversations have become aversive recycling of unwinnable 'what did we mean' disputes, avoiding them is locally rational. But the avoidance could equally be about something else — the friendship, feeling policed, life outside the flat — and the material cannot tell these apart. Both readings, though, point to the same first move: change the format of coordination so it costs less, and ask rather than diagnose.

What the asker can actually do, with two co-decision-makers and one of them withdrawing, is propose, not enforce.

First, stop litigating the past. What an ambiguous agreement meant cannot be reconstructed, only superseded. Say once, at a calm moment, that old disputed agreements are off the table and future ones start fresh — then hold to it, even when relitigating would feel satisfying.

Second, make the next agreements checkable. One shared place — a whiteboard, a shared note, an app — where every agreement names the task, the owner, a deadline, and one line on what 'done' looks like. The point is shared memory, not surveillance, and offering it as a two-week trial lets the others amend or drop it rather than resist it.

Third, build the schedules in. A standing rule: if your schedule changes and you can't do what you claimed, say so by an agreed day and it gets re-dealt. This gives silence somewhere to go besides defiance, and makes the system bend with the very constraint that keeps breaking it.

Fourth, re-approach the avoidant friend at their cost level: ask which format they would actually tolerate — a ten-minute, time-boxed check-in, or messages if that is what they will answer — and offer the trial in that form, framed as making life easier for everyone rather than holding anyone to account. Asking also gathers information about why they avoid, without forcing a diagnosis on them.

Three failure modes deserve naming. A written system among friends can read as distrust, and the record can be repurposed as a charge sheet; the mitigations are the trial framing, a light tone, and an explicit norm that the board is a memory aid, not evidence. Whoever runs the system has acquired a new unrecorded chore — if that is the asker alone, the fix breeds the resentment it was meant to cure, so facilitation should rotate. And most important: if the real issue is that one person in fact does much more, or if the avoidance is about the friendship with chores merely where it surfaces, tidier coordination will not touch it, and the honest move is a different conversation, at a calm moment unrelated to any dispute. This account cannot tell which situation the asker is in; only they can check. The two-week trial doubles as a diagnostic — if a clean slate, a shared record, and a cheap exit route do not reduce the friction, that is evidence the problem was never about the form of the agreements at all.

## Selected input objection (p.response.1)
[9420677de8893e01] (h005.fork5.p.response.1)
Source objection: daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/objection; selected view: both
Artifact: 3124874b846e0e04976e405b86fe6e4d9bf84b3dea24902791e43c26e539e1b7
Original body SHA256: 3b1267166dceab12e86d4b2fe166c85e8a49e61e8ede85e225c3ffb15cd2dbb0

BODY
The account is unusually honest about its conjectures, names three of its failure modes itself, and answers in the right register — propose, don't enforce. My objections are therefore about execution rather than posture: one framing inference, one internal inconsistency, an interaction between two of its own named risks, an over-read diagnostic, and three omissions, in rough order of confidence.

1. The headline conjecture presents rivals where there is likely a conjunction. 'Not primarily a fairness fight but an ambiguity problem wearing a fairness fight's clothes' treats fairness and ambiguity as competing diagnoses. But in shared housing, meaning-disputes are the ordinary medium of fairness fights: people who judge the load uneven contest the meaning of agreements they would honour under a fairer split. Underspecification explains the form the disputes take; it does not by itself explain their persistence and heat — and persistence, heat, and one party now avoiding the topic altogether are what the material actually reports. Pure coordination failure tends to produce irritation and workarounds; it less commonly produces avoidance. I cannot prove the grievance-through-ambiguity reading is correct; the narrower point is harder to deflect: the exclusivity in the framing is unearned, and it is load-bearing for everything downstream.

2. The sequencing follows from that unearned exclusivity, and the account never designs the cheapest test of the hypothesis it says it cannot rule out. It admits (r11, its open problem on distributive fairness) that whether the issue is distributive cannot be determined, yet runs the coordination trial first and places the 'different conversation' only in the conditional branch where its diagnosis turned out wrong. A one-to-two-week tally of who actually did what needs no consent, no system, no conversation, and fits inside the same fortnight; it can stay private, used only to check the asker's own assumption of what 'we all do roughly equally' amounts to. Its omission means the trial does all its diagnostic work on the form-hypothesis and none on the load-hypothesis. Notice the direction of that asymmetry: the diagnosis the account privileges — it's technique, not fairness — is precisely the one most comfortable for the asker to receive. An adviser should be suspicious of a diagnosis that flatters its recipient and should spend at least equal effort designing the test of the unflattering one.

3. r3 and r5 are inconsistent about power. r3 grants the asker proposal-only standing. r5 has the asker declare that old disputed agreements are off the table, then 'hold to it'. Declaring what is discussable for all three is not a proposal; it is a unilateral adjournment of other people's grievances. If any flatmate's sense of unfairness rests on the past — they believe they carried the loose arrangements — a clean slate decreed by one member reads as amnesty engineered by whoever the record would have disadvantaged, and will be received as frame-rigging whatever its intent. The defensible core of r5 is narrower and the account should say so: the asker may decline to defend their own past interpretations and may offer supersession as a proposal; they may not adjourn topics for the others. Relatedly, 'what an ambiguous agreement meant cannot be reconstructed, only superseded' is epistemically overstated — contemporaneous messages and shared context often partially reconstruct it — and there is an odd asymmetry in the account's own epistemology: the past pattern is admissible as evidence for the diagnosis (r1's grounds lean on it) while being ruled unreconstructable inside the flat.

4. Two failure modes the account lists separately interact in a way it never traces. r9 worries the record could be repurposed as a charge sheet. r7 gives silence an exit — but only for schedule-based silence. r4 says the cause of the avoidance is undetermined. Put them together: a persistent, visible record with the friend's name, a task and a deadline documents non-performance in real time, in shared space, where memory used to be vague. If the friend's avoidance is about anything other than scheduling — which r4 explicitly leaves open — the board makes their silence more, not less, legible as defiance and hands the others a running exhibit. The account names both risks but never multiplies them; its claim that the system 'gives silence somewhere to go besides defiance' holds only for one species of silence and may invert for the other.

5. The asking is mis-specified. The slogan is 'ask rather than diagnose', but every question the account proposes to the friend is a format question — ten minutes, or messages? — which reveals cost tolerance, not reason. r8's claim that the asking 'gathers information about why they avoid' holds only if the friend volunteers it. A person who has begun avoiding these conversations may be waiting to be asked a different question — what's wrong, what would make these worth having, what doesn't feel fair — and being asked only about scheduling mechanics may confirm their sense that the real subject is being managed around. There is also a frame-function gap: the offer is to be framed 'as convenience rather than accountability' while the body concedes the trial 'doubles as a diagnostic' — of the friend. Avoidant people are often expert at detecting exactly this gap, and the account gives no guidance for the moment when the friend asks why the asker is really doing this.

6. The trial cannot bear the epistemic weight of the closing claim. If a clean slate, a record, and an exit route do not reduce friction, that is allegedly evidence the problem was 'never about the form of the agreements at all'. A null result is evidence against the form-hypothesis only conditional on adequate implementation, genuine uptake by all three, and sufficient duration — none ensured: the record may be run in the distrust key (r9), upkeep may fall on one person (r10), the friend may never engage, and two weeks is short for a new coordination habit to displace an entrenched conflict pattern even when the diagnosis is right. Symmetrically, a calm fortnight may be novelty. The trial is a reasonable intervention and an unreliable instrument; the account conflates the two.

7. There is no branch for non-uptake, and the framing hands the avoidant friend a veto they never asked for. Every move presupposes the friend will at least entertain a format; the described avoidance makes non-engagement a live and likely outcome, and the account says nothing about what the asker does then. r3's 'a system only works if offered as something the others can accept' also overlooks that with three residents, the asker plus the willing friend are a working majority for their own arrangements: a partial record covering two of three, the third invited and never compelled, lowers the stakes and leaves the offer open without depending on the one person least likely to accept it. As written, the avoidant friend's silence blocks the asker's coordination with the third flatmate — a veto their avoidance effectively exercises.

8. The account never considers that the asker might be the problem party. r11 asks whether one person in fact does much more, but the possibility that this person is the asker is never raised; no move has the asker solicit feedback about their own conduct; the questions proposed to the others concern format and tolerance, never what they wish the asker did differently. Self-report is systematically charitable to the reporter, and a first-person task statement is no exception. If the asker is the under-contributor — or the over-policer, a possibility r9 raises in the abstract without ever turning it on the asker — then the facilitator-designer role the account assigns them is tactically convenient, and the designer's sense of what counts as 'done' quietly sets the terms. The remedy costs one line: track the asker's own items on the same record and invite the other two to flag them.

Where these objections might themselves be wrong. Point 1 rests on a generalisation I cannot verify — that coordination failure produces irritation rather than avoidance; sustained unwinnable memory-disputes may be aversive enough to produce avoidance on their own, in which case 1 collapses to the weaker but still standing claim that the exclusivity is unearned. Against 3, the account may reply that declining to engage with past claims is mere personal consistency within anyone's rights; my harm allegation depends on others actually holding past-based grievances, which the material leaves undetermined. Against 5, format questions may be exactly right as low-stakes openers; my claim is only that they do not do the information-gathering work r8 assigns them. The account already anticipates r9, r10 and r11; my charge is not that these were missed but that their joint implications (points 1 and 4) were not drawn, and that the cheapest test of r11 was never designed (point 2).

BODY
The material exposes five facts: three people share a flat; they argue about chores; they sometimes agree who will do something and later disagree about what the agreement meant; their schedules change; one friend has begun avoiding the conversations. Nothing about effort shares, about whether agreements were spoken or written, or about why the friend avoids is stated. What follows is one conjecture among several the facts permit, offered as a rival to the selected account's reading.

That account reads the recurring meaning-disputes as missing specification: agreements that fixed who but not when, to what standard, under what conditions, so each party later fills in the missing halves sincerely and differently. Its remedy is to make future agreements checkable — one shared place naming the task, the owner, a deadline, and a line on what "done" means.

Here is a rival reading. The problem may not be that the agreements are underspecified but that there are so many of them. Chore-by-chore negotiation among equals is an expensive format: each round costs a proposal, a memory, an interpretation, and, when memories diverge, a litigation. Nobody in this flat can compel anybody; the only currency is goodwill, and every disputed micro-agreement is paid for out of the same goodwill that motivates the chores themselves. On this reading, the fights about "what we meant" are the litigation phase of tiny contracts, and they recur despite everyone's apparent sincerity because the format generates them. The fix is not better contracts but fewer: replace negotiated agreement with structures that need no fresh consent per task.

Two structures do that. Domains: each person owns whole areas outright — kitchen, bathroom, bins, whatever the flat's work actually is — with autonomy over how and when, so the only shared agreement is the boundary, made once and disputed rarely. Rotation: a fixed cycle that runs by default, so nobody proposes anything; a changed roster becomes a one-line swap between two people rather than a household renegotiation. In both, the surface for interpretive disagreement shrinks from many small fights to occasional boundary questions.

The record-keeping remedy, on this reading, has a specific flaw: it does not remove negotiation, it relocates it. Entries get contested at the margin — you wrote "bathroom," but did that include the floor? — the clerk role gets contested (the selected account sees this and rotates it), and documented shortfall among friends raises stakes rather than lowering them. That account anticipates the charge-sheet risk and mitigates it with trial framing and a memory-aid norm; the rival point is that even a benign, well-run record leaves the negotiation volume intact, changing only what gets negotiated. Every added specification is one more thing to dispute when a roster changes.

The avoidant friend, under the rival reading, is avoiding not chores but meetings. The offer to make is participation at near-zero conversational cost: a domain of their own, or a rotation slot, chosen by preference where possible and swappable by message. The question to ask is a preference question — "which would you hate least" — not a negotiation. If avoidance persists even when there are no meetings to avoid, that is informative: it was never about the format.

Three honest limits. Domains are rarely equal, and a first allocation can quietly entrench inequity, so it needs one rough workload check, done once at a calm moment and then left alone for the trial's duration — otherwise the structure reopens the fairness fight it was meant to bypass. Some coordination really is irreducible — bills, guests, shared purchases — and there the selected account's records and renegotiation rules have their proper place; the two accounts are complementary about different parts of the work, not exclusive. And decisively: whether the friction is about coordination volume or about standing — who is respected, who is taken for granted — is not decidable from the exposed facts. The structure trial is a diagnostic as much as a treatment, and here the two accounts converge from opposite sides. If removing negotiation does not reduce the friction, the household has learned something tidier coordination was masking, and the next conversation is one no system can hold for them.
